etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English relaxen, from Old French relaxer, from Latin relaxāre (“relax, loosen, open”), from re- (“back”) + laxāre (“loosen”), from laxus (“loose, free”).

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VIII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:

quote.text:
I relax in the living room.
Audio (US):(file)

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make something less severe or tense.
(intransitive) To become less severe or tense.
(transitive) To make something (such as codes and regulations) more lenient.

quote.citation: 1713, Jonathan Swift, A Preface to Bishop Burnet's Introduction:
quote.text: The statute of mortmain […]  was at several times relaxed by the legislature.

quote.citation: 1953, “Section 2. Jurisdiction”, in Edward Samuel Corwin, editor, The Constitution of the United States of America: Analysis and Interpretation‎[1], page 589:
quote.text: The Court rejected the contention that the doctrine of sovereign immunity should be relaxed as inapplicable to suits for specific relief as distinguished from damage suits, saying: "The Government, as representative of the community as a whole, cannot be stopped in its tracks by any plaintiff who presents a disputed question of property or contract right."

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of codes and regulations) To become more lenient.
(transitive, dated) To relieve from constipation; to loosen; to open.
